**Test 1, 23 December 2024** (EEU 08104 Power Electronics Design, 90 minutes). The questions are retyped from the paper; the original scan is under Past papers. Every answer was re-solved and checked numerically. Try each question before opening its answer.

## Q1(a) Battery charger through a diode
A 12 V battery is charged by a single-phase, single-pulse (half-wave) diode rectifier. The supply is 40 V, 50 Hz. Determine the resistance to insert in series with the battery to limit the **average** charging current to 6 A. Take a voltage drop of 1 V across the diode, and derive all the expressions you use.

::: answer
**Set-up.** $v_s = V_m\sin\theta$ with $\theta = \omega t$ and $V_m = \sqrt2 \times 40 = 56.57$ V. The diode can only conduct while the supply exceeds the battery voltage plus the diode drop, $E' = 12 + 1 = 13$ V. While it conducts,

$$i(\theta) = \frac{V_m\sin\theta - E'}{R}$$

**Conduction angles.** Conduction starts at $\theta_1$, where $V_m\sin\theta_1 = E'$, and stops at $\theta_2 = \pi - \theta_1$ (the resistor has no inductance, so the current stops as soon as $v_s$ falls back to $E'$):

$$\theta_1 = \sin^{-1}\frac{E'}{V_m} = \sin^{-1}\frac{13}{56.57} = 13.29°$$

that is, 0.2319 rad, and $\theta_2 = 166.71°$.

**Average current.**

$$\begin{gathered}I_{av} = \frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{\theta_1}^{\pi - \theta_1}\frac{V_m\sin\theta - E'}{R}\,d\theta \\ = \frac{1}{2\pi R}\Big[-V_m\cos\theta - E'\theta\Big]_{\theta_1}^{\pi - \theta_1}\end{gathered}$$

$$\boxed{I_{av} = \frac{1}{2\pi R}\Big[2V_m\cos\theta_1 - E'(\pi - 2\theta_1)\Big]}$$

(The same thing written as $\frac{1}{2\pi R}[2V_m\cos\theta_1 + 2E'\theta_1 - E'\pi]$.)

**Numbers.** $2V_m\cos\theta_1 = 2 \times 56.57 \times 0.9732 = 110.11$; $E'(\pi - 2\theta_1) = 13 \times 2.6778 = 34.81$. So

$$R = \frac{110.11 - 34.81}{2\pi \times 6} = \frac{75.30}{37.70} = 2.0\ \Omega$$

**Check** (numerical integration of $i(\theta)$ with $R = 2.0\ \Omega$): $I_{av} = 6.00$ A. *Not asked, but useful:* the rms current is 10.2 A, so the resistor dissipates $10.17^2 \times 2.0 = 206$ W while the battery receives only $12 \times 6 = 72$ W and the diode 6 W. Resistive charging is wasteful.
:::

## Q1(b) Half-wave controlled rectifier, resistive load
A half-wave phase-controlled rectifier has a 20 Ω resistive load and a 240 V rms, 50 Hz source, and operates with α = 40°. Find (i) the peak load voltage, (ii) the peak load current, (iii) the average load voltage, (iv) the average load current, (v) the rms load current, (vi) the power to the load.

::: answer
The thyristor conducts from $\alpha$ to $\pi$, and $v_o = V_m\sin\omega t$ while it conducts.

1. $V_m = \sqrt2 \times 240 = 339.4$ V.
2. $I_m = V_m/R = 339.4/20 = 16.97$ A.
3. $V_{av} = \dfrac{1}{2\pi}\displaystyle\int_\alpha^\pi V_m\sin\theta\,d\theta = \dfrac{V_m}{2\pi}(1 + \cos\alpha) = \dfrac{339.4}{2\pi}(1 + 0.766) = 95.4$ V.
4. $I_{av} = V_{av}/R = 4.77$ A.
5. $I_{rms} = \left[\dfrac{1}{2\pi}\displaystyle\int_\alpha^\pi I_m^2\sin^2\theta\,d\theta\right]^{1/2} = \dfrac{I_m}{2}\left[1 - \dfrac{\alpha}{\pi} + \dfrac{\sin2\alpha}{2\pi}\right]^{1/2} = 8.485 \times (1 - 0.2222 + 0.1567)^{1/2} = 8.20$ A.
6. $P = I_{rms}^2R = 8.203^2 \times 20 = 1346$ W (1345 W if you square the rounded 8.20 A).
:::

## Q2 Three-phase diode bridge (20 marks)
A three-phase bridge rectifier has a purely resistive load R. It delivers $I_{dc} = 60$ A at $V_{dc} = 280.7$ V, and the source frequency is 50 Hz. Determine (i) the efficiency, (ii) the peak inverse voltage of each diode, (iii) the peak current through a diode.

::: answer
$R = 280.7/60 = 4.678\ \Omega$; $P_{dc} = 280.7 \times 60 = 16\,842$ W.

The output follows the largest line voltage. With $V_m$ the peak **phase** voltage, $V_{dc} = \dfrac{3\sqrt3}{\pi}V_m = 1.6540V_m$ and $V_{rms} = 1.6554V_m$.

**(i)** $V_m = 280.7/1.6540 = 169.7$ V; $V_{rms} = 1.6554 \times 169.7 = 280.9$ V.

$$\eta = \frac{P_{dc}}{P_{ac}} = \frac{V_{dc}^2/R}{V_{rms}^2/R} = \left(\frac{1.6540}{1.6554}\right)^2 = 99.83\%$$

**(ii)** Each diode must block the peak line voltage: $PIV = \sqrt3V_m = \sqrt3 \times 169.7 = 293.9$ V.

**(iii)** The peak output current flows through the conducting diodes: $I_m = \dfrac{\sqrt3V_m}{R} = \dfrac{293.9}{4.678} = 62.8$ A. (Each diode conducts for 120°, so its average current is $I_{dc}/3 = 20$ A.)
:::

## Q3(a) Buck chopper with a small inductor
A buck chopper operates at 20 kHz with L = 10 µH. The output capacitance is large and the input is 40 V DC. The output is regulated at 30 V and the converter supplies a 200 W load. Find (i) the duty ratio, (ii) the peak inductor current, (iii) plot the capacitor current, (iv) the output voltage at which the inductor current becomes continuous.

::: answer
$I_o = 200/30 = 6.67$ A; $R = 30/6.67 = 4.5\ \Omega$; $T = 1/20\,000 = 50\ \mu$s.

**Check the mode first.** If the current were continuous, $\delta = 30/40 = 0.75$ and the critical inductance would be

$$L_{crit} = \frac{(1 - \delta)R}{2f} = \frac{0.25 \times 4.5}{2 \times 20\,000} = 28.1\ \mu\text{H}$$

The actual 10 µH is smaller, so the inductor current is **discontinuous** and $\delta$ is *not* $V_o/E$.

**(i) Duty ratio (DCM).** During $\delta T$ the current rises from zero: $I_{max} = \dfrac{E - V_o}{L}\delta T = \dfrac{10 \times 50\ \mu s}{10\ \mu H}\delta = 50\delta$ A. The source supplies current only while the switch is on, a triangle of average $I_{max}\delta/2$, so the power balance is

$$\begin{gathered}E\,\frac{I_{max}\delta}{2} = P_o \;\Rightarrow\; 40 \times \frac{50\delta^2}{2} = 200 \\ \delta^2 = 0.2, \quad \boxed{\delta = 0.447}\end{gathered}$$

Same answer from the chapter's DCM formula: $V_o/E = K[-1 + \sqrt{1 + 2/K}] = 0.75$ gives $K = 1.125$, and $K = \dfrac{TR\delta^2}{4L} = 5.625\delta^2$, so $\delta = 0.447$.

**(ii) Peak inductor current.** $I_{max} = 50 \times 0.447 = 22.4$ A.

The current then falls at $V_o/L$ and reaches zero after $\dfrac{LI_{max}}{V_o} = \dfrac{10\ \mu H \times 22.36}{30} = 7.45\ \mu$s, at $\delta_2T = 22.36 + 7.45 = 29.8\ \mu$s ($\delta_2 = 0.596$). It stays at zero until 50 µs. Check: average $i_L = \frac12 \times 22.36 \times 0.596 = 6.67$ A $= I_o$. ✓

**(iii) Capacitor current.** $i_C = i_L - I_o$:

- from 0 to 22.4 µs it rises from −6.67 A to $22.36 - 6.67 = +15.7$ A (crossing zero at 6.67 µs);
- from 22.4 to 29.8 µs it falls back to −6.67 A (crossing zero at 27.6 µs);
- from 29.8 to 50 µs it stays at −6.67 A, while the capacitor alone feeds the load.

Bottom: i<sub>C</sub> = i<sub>L</sub> − I<sub>o</sub>, from +15.7 A down to −6.67 A. The two areas are equal, so the average capacitor current is zero.</figcaption></figure>

**(iv) Boundary of continuous conduction.** Keeping the same 4.5 Ω load and raising $\delta$, the current just becomes continuous when $L = L_{crit}$:

$$\begin{gathered}10\ \mu\text{H} = \frac{(1 - \delta)\,4.5}{2 \times 20\,000} \\ 1 - \delta = 0.0889, \quad \delta = 0.911\end{gathered}$$

$$V_o = \delta E = 0.911 \times 40 = 36.4 \text{ V}$$

Above about 36.4 V the inductor current is continuous. (The DCM formula gives the same value at $\delta = 0.911$, as it must at the boundary.)

*If instead the load power is held at 200 W* (so $R$ changes with $V_o$), the boundary is where $\Delta I_L/2 = I_o$: $\dfrac{(40 - V_o)(V_o/40)T}{2L} = \dfrac{200}{V_o}$, i.e. $(40 - V_o)V_o^2 = 3200$, giving $V_o = 37.8$ V. State which reading you use.
:::

## Q3(b) Boost converter design
Design a boost DC–DC converter that gives 27 W at 40 V with an output ripple of 2%. The input is 28 V and the switching frequency is 35 kHz. Assume continuous conduction.

::: answer
**Duty ratio.** $V_o = \dfrac{V_{in}}{1 - D}$, so $D = 1 - \dfrac{28}{40} = 0.3$.

**Load.** $R = \dfrac{V_o^2}{P} = \dfrac{1600}{27} = 59.26\ \Omega$; $I_o = 40/59.26 = 0.675$ A.

**Inductor.** The minimum inductance for continuous current is

$$L_{min} = \frac{D(1 - D)^2R}{2f} = \frac{0.3 \times 0.49 \times 59.26}{2 \times 35\,000} = 124\ \mu\text{H}$$

Choose a larger value to stay safely continuous, say **L = 200 µH**. Then $I_L = \dfrac{I_o}{1 - D} = 0.964$ A, $\Delta I_L = \dfrac{V_{in}D}{Lf} = \dfrac{28 \times 0.3}{200\ \mu H \times 35\,000} = 1.2$ A, so $I_{max} = 1.56$ A and $I_{min} = 0.36$ A > 0. ✓

**Capacitor.** The capacitor alone feeds the load during $DT$, so $\dfrac{\Delta V_o}{V_o} = \dfrac{D}{RCf}$:

$$C = \frac{D}{Rf(\Delta V_o/V_o)} = \frac{0.3}{59.26 \times 35\,000 \times 0.02} = 7.23\ \mu\text{F}$$

**Design:** D = 0.3, L = 200 µH (minimum 124 µH), C ≥ 7.2 µF, switch and diode rated for at least 1.6 A and 40 V.
:::

## Q4(a) Buck-boost converter at two outputs
A buck-boost converter supplies a variable voltage to a 15 Ω resistive load from a 20 V source. With the output at 30 V the inductor current is just continuous. Find the operating conditions at an output of 15 V, with f = 50 kHz.

::: answer
Take $f = 50$ kHz in both cases ($T = 20\ \mu$s), and output magnitudes.

**Find L from the 30 V condition.** In CCM $|V_o| = \dfrac{\delta E}{1 - \delta}$, so $\delta = \dfrac{|V_o|}{|V_o| + E} = \dfrac{30}{50} = 0.6$. "Just continuous" means $L$ equals the critical value:

$$L = L_{crit} = \frac{(1 - \delta)^2R}{2f} = \frac{0.16 \times 15}{2 \times 50\,000} = 24\ \mu\text{H}$$

(Check: $I_o = 2$ A, average $I_L = I_o/(1 - \delta) = 5$ A, ripple $\Delta I = E\delta T/L = 10$ A, so $I_{min} = 0$ and $I_{max} = 10$ A.)

**Is 15 V continuous?** In CCM it would need $\delta = 15/35 = 0.429$, and then $L_{crit} = \dfrac{0.571^2 \times 15}{100\,000} = 49\ \mu$H > 24 µH. So at 15 V the current is **discontinuous**.

**DCM relation.** The current rises from zero to $I_{max} = E\delta T/L$ while the switch is on; all the energy $\frac12LI_{max}^2$ stored each cycle is passed to the load:

$$\begin{gathered}\tfrac12LI_{max}^2 f = \frac{V_o^2}{R} \;\Rightarrow\; \frac{E^2\delta^2T}{2L} = \frac{V_o^2}{R} \\ \boxed{V_o = E\delta\sqrt{\frac{RT}{2L}}}\end{gathered}$$

**Operating conditions at 15 V.** $\sqrt{RT/2L} = \sqrt{\dfrac{15 \times 20\ \mu s}{48\ \mu H}} = 2.5$, so

- duty ratio $\delta = \dfrac{15}{20 \times 2.5} = 0.30$ (on-time 6 µs);
- peak inductor (and switch) current $I_{max} = \dfrac{20 \times 0.3 \times 20\ \mu s}{24\ \mu H} = 5$ A;
- the current falls at $V_o/L$ and reaches zero after $\dfrac{LI_{max}}{V_o} = \dfrac{24 \times 5}{15} = 8\ \mu$s, at $t = 14\ \mu$s ($\delta_2 = 0.7$); it is **zero for the last 6 µs** of each period;
- load current $I_o = 1$ A = average diode current $\frac12 \times 5 \times 0.4$ ✓;
- average source current $\frac12 \times 5 \times 0.3 = 0.75$ A, so $P_{in} = 15$ W $= V_o^2/R$ ✓.
:::

Energy moves from input to output through the series capacitor C<sub>1</sub>. Both the input and the output have an inductor, so both currents are smooth. V<sub>o</sub> = −δE/(1 − δ).</figcaption></figure>

Assume continuous conduction, large capacitors (constant $V_{C1}$ and $V_o = V_{C2}$) and an ideal switch and diode. In steady state each inductor's average voltage is zero (volt-second balance).

**Switch on** ($0 < t < \delta T$): the diode is reverse-biased by $C_1$.

- Loop 1: $v_{L1} = E$, so $i_{L1}$ rises.
- Loop 2: $C_1$ discharges through the switch into $L_2$ and the load: $v_{L2} = -V_{C1} - V_{C2}$.

**Switch off** ($\delta T < t < T$): the diode conducts.

- Loop 1: $E = v_{L1} + V_{C1}$, so $v_{L1} = E - V_{C1}$ and $C_1$ is recharged from the input.
- Loop 2: $v_{L2} + V_{C2} = 0$.

**Volt-second balance on $L_1$:** $E\delta + (E - V_{C1})(1 - \delta) = 0 \Rightarrow V_{C1} = \dfrac{E}{1 - \delta}$.

**Volt-second balance on $L_2$:** $(-V_{C1} - V_{C2})\delta + (-V_{C2})(1 - \delta) = 0 \Rightarrow V_{C2} = -\delta V_{C1}$.

Combining:

$$\boxed{V_o = V_{C2} = -\frac{\delta}{1 - \delta}E}$$

The output is inverted and can be lower ($\delta < 0.5$) or higher ($\delta > 0.5$) than the input, like the buck-boost converter. $C_1$ must be rated for $E + |V_o|$.

on</text><text x="247.5" y="12" text-anchor="middle" class="d-t s m">S off</text></svg><figcaption>Ćuk converter currents in continuous conduction (δ = 0.4). Both inductor currents rise while S is on and fall while it is off. The switch carries i<sub>L1</sub> + i<sub>L2</sub> while on; the diode carries i<sub>L1</sub> + i<sub>L2</sub> while S is off. The input and output currents (i<sub>L1</sub>, i<sub>L2</sub>) are continuous, which is the Ćuk converter's advantage.</figcaption></figure>

- $i_{L1}$ (input current) and $i_{L2}$ (output current): triangles around their averages, rising during $\delta T$ and falling during $(1 - \delta)T$; both continuous.
- Switch: carries $i_{L1} + i_{L2}$ while on, zero while off.
- Diode: zero while the switch is on, $i_{L1} + i_{L2}$ while it is off.
- Average values (lossless): $I_{L1} = I_{in}$, $I_{L2} = I_o$, with $EI_{L1} = |V_o|I_{L2}$.
